strengths: The paper addresses an important PEFT trade-off and proposes a clear Tucker-like tensor parameterization in which random factors/core are frozen while only small diagonal scaling vectors are trained, decoupling update-matrix rank from the number of trainable parameters.
The method is practically attractive: the tensorized adapter can be unfolded and merged into the base weights, introducing no additional inference latency or computation.

The paper complements the method with formal analysis of the attainable rank, trainable-parameter count under full-rank tensorization, and approximation error, giving a principled account of the parameter-efficiency/expressivity trade-off.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably broad, covering commonsense reasoning, personalized dialogue, and arithmetic reasoning on Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B, with comparisons to LoRA, HiRA, VeRA, LoRETTA, and prompt-based methods. TeRA performs strongly at very low trainable-parameter budgets.

Rank visualizations and ablations on tensorization choices and random versus identity initialization directly support the main design claims. The paper is generally well organized and the figures help explain the method.
weaknesses: The efficiency analysis focuses almost exclusively on trainable parameters. When R_i = I_i, the frozen core itself has O(J1J2) entries, and the frozen factor matrices also add storage/memory. The paper does not report total adapter memory, training FLOPs, runtime, or how the shared random tensors are materialized.

High matrix rank is not equivalent to high expressive power. TeRA still has only sum_i R_i trainable degrees of freedom and restricts updates to a randomly parameterized subspace. The extreme high-order configurations with very few trainable scalars are not shown to be empirically effective; the main results use a substantially less extreme parameterization.

The parameter-efficiency theorem is narrower than some prose suggests. It counts trainable parameters under specific factorization assumptions and does not account for frozen parameters or methods such as HiRA, whose Hadamard product with W_0 can yield a full-rank update even with r=1.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The exact tensor shapes used for the main model/task configurations, learning rate, batch size, sequence length, random seeds, core/factor sharing rules, and code availability are not fully specified.

Although results are averaged over five runs, standard deviations and statistical significance are omitted. This matters for close comparisons such as the Llama-3 commonsense result, where TeRA and HiRA(r=32) have the same reported average.

The evaluation would be strengthened by runtime/memory comparisons and by more diverse instruction-following or open-ended generation benchmarks, which would better establish that the gains generalize beyond the reported tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important trade-off in PEFT. TeRA is conceptually simple: tensorize the weight update, use a Tucker-like network with frozen shared random factors and core, and train only layer-specific diagonal scaling vectors. The resulting update can be merged into the base weights, yielding zero inference overhead.

The theoretical analysis is more complete than in many PEFT papers. The rank bound, full-rank parameter-efficiency comparison, and approximation-error analysis clarify both the capacity and limitations of the method, with proofs supplied in the appendix.

Empirical results are strong across three substantially different settings—commonsense reasoning, personalized dialogue generation, and arithmetic reasoning—using both Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B. TeRA consistently offers a favorable accuracy-vs-trainable-parameter trade-off against a broad set of baselines.

The evaluation includes useful ablations on tensorization strategy, adapter placement, random versus identity initialization, sharing of frozen components, higher-rank LoRA/HiRA variants, and additional competing methods. Rank visualizations also directly support the high-rank claim.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with informative diagrams, a notation table, hyperparameter and hardware details, results over five runs, statistical tests, and a stated code release.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: TeRA can be viewed as a higher-order, Tucker-based extension of VeRA-style frozen random factors with trainable diagonal scaling. The paper would benefit from a sharper explanation of why this is more than a natural tensorization of an existing vector-based design.

Matrix rank alone is only a coarse measure of useful expressivity. With random full-rank factors and nonzero diagonal entries, full rank is almost guaranteed. Effective rank, singular-value spectra, or more targeted ablations would better substantiate the claim that high rank produces meaningfully more useful adaptations.

The most dramatic parameter-saving tensorizations in the theoretical discussion are not the configurations that work best empirically. The strong practical results retain a 4096-dimensional mode, while tensorizing both dimensions substantially hurts performance, so the extremely low-parameter regimes should not be presented as readily achievable.

A few claims are slightly overstated. For example, on Llama-2-7B Commonsense170k, TeRA averages 78.63 versus HiRA (r=32) at 79.97, so it does not exactly match that baseline there; on Llama-3-8B, VeRA uses fewer trainable parameters than TeRA. These distinctions should be stated precisely.

Training efficiency is not directly quantified. Although inference is overhead-free, the paper does not report wall-clock time, peak memory, or the computational cost of tensor contractions and storing/materializing the frozen random tensors during adaptation.

Reproducibility is good but not fully self-contained: standard deviations or confidence intervals are omitted from the main tables, and seeds, epochs, the exact selected learning rate for each experiment, and baseline hyperparameter-search procedures are not clearly specified.
